components.note: 亻 (person) plus 尔 (an old second-person pronoun) — combines to form 你, the modern word for 'you.'
宀 (roof) — 家 is about a home, the space under a roof.
豕 (shǐ, 'pig') supplies the ancient sound for 家; keeping a pig under one's roof was also a practical sign of a household in ancient China, though the modern readings jiā and shǐ no longer rhyme.

example.hanzi: 你家有几个人?
example.pinyin: Nǐjiā yǒu jǐ gè rén?
example.english: How many people are in your family?
example.fact: 你家 attaches the possessive 你 ("you") directly onto 家 ("home/family") with no linking word — Mandarin regularly drops 的 between a pronoun and a close relationship or possession, a compression that English's "your" + noun does not allow.

components.note: 一 (a line, representing a target or standard) — 正 shows a foot arriving exactly at the right mark.
止 (foot, to stop) — arriving and stopping precisely at the target gives 正 its meaning of 'correct' or 'straight.'
⺷ (sheep, related to 羊) — 义 relates to what is right or moral, linked to the idea of sacrificial sheep used in rituals of righteousness.
乂 (yì) gives the sound — 义 is also pronounced yì, an exact match.

example.hanzi: 他相信正义终将战胜邪恶。
example.pinyin: Tā xiāngxìn zhèngyì zhōng jiāng zhànshèng xié'è.
example.english: He believes justice will ultimately triumph over evil.
example.fact: 正 already means "correct, upright" on its own (as in 正确, "correct"), and 义 means "righteousness, moral duty" — 正义 layers two near-synonymous "rightness" characters together, the same doubling strategy behind 喜欢 in the pilot batch.

components.note: 网 depicts a woven mesh net stretched over a frame — a picture of a fishing or hunting net, giving 网 its meaning 'net, network.'
立 (to stand) — 站 relates to standing, and by extension a stop or station where one stands to wait
占 (zhàn) gives the sound — 站 is also pronounced zhàn, an exact match

example.hanzi: 这个网站的信息很有用。
example.pinyin: Zhège wǎngzhàn de xìnxī hěn yǒuyòng.
example.english: This website's information is very useful.
example.fact: 网站 is a modern coinage built from two older characters — 网 ("net," a woven hunting or fishing net) supplies the metaphor for a network, and 站 ("station," as in a bus or train stop) supplies the idea of a fixed point one arrives at — giving Chinese a compositional equivalent of "website" rather than a phonetic loanword.

meanings: (after a noun) place where it is located

components.note: 户 (door) — 所 evokes a location or place, such as where a door stands.
斤 (axe) — combined with 户 (door), the image of an axe at a door gave rise to the abstract sense of 'a place' or 'that which.'
土 (earth/soil) — 在 originally related to standing on the ground
才 (cái) gives the sound — 在 is pronounced zài, a close match

example.hanzi: 这就是问题的所在。
example.pinyin: Zhè jiùshì wèntí de suǒzài.
example.english: This is exactly where the problem lies.
example.fact: 所 is a grammatical marker that turns a following verb into a noun-like "that which is [verb]ed" — attached to 在 ("to be located at"), 所在 literally means "that which is located," which is why it almost always trails a noun with 的 (问题的所在, "where the problem lies") rather than standing alone as an ordinary place word like 这里.

components.note: 彡 (shān) is the historical phonetic component of 参; sound change over time has left little resemblance to the modern reading cān
讠 (speech) — relates to 议's meaning 'to discuss, deliberate; opinion.'
义 (yì) gives the sound — 议 is also pronounced yì, an exact match.
贝 (shell/money — cowrie shells were historically used as currency) — 员 originally related to counting or officials responsible for accounts, later broadening to mean 'member' or 'personnel.'

example.hanzi: 这位参议员支持这项新法律。
example.pinyin: Zhè wèi cānyìyuán zhīchí zhè xiàng xīn fǎlǜ.
example.english: This senator supports this new law.
example.fact: 参议员 names a member of an upper legislative chamber generically — 参 ("to participate") + 议 ("to deliberate") + 员 ("member") — so it applies just as naturally to a U.S. senator as to a member of a "参议院" in another bicameral system, rather than being tied to one specific country.

components.note: 凵 depicts an open container or pit, shown here holding something dangerous inside.
乂 is a crossed mark suggesting something tangled or harmful — trapped inside the container 凵, it gives 凶 its meaning 'vicious, ominous.'
口 (a vessel), shown four times — a set of cooking vessels.
犬 (a dog) — guarding the vessels, the source of 器's meaning 'vessel, tool, instrument.'

example.hanzi: 警察在现场找到了凶器。
example.pinyin: Jǐngchá zài xiànchǎng zhǎodào le xiōngqì.
example.english: The police found the murder weapon at the scene.
example.fact: 凶 by itself means "fierce, ominous, deadly" (as in 凶手, "murderer"), and 器 means "tool, instrument" — 凶器 is a fully transparent compound, literally "a deadly tool," making it one of the easier crime-vocabulary words for a learner to reconstruct from its parts.

components.note: 尺 (a ruler/measure) — represents rules or measures being set.
口 (mouth) — measures being discussed aloud in one place gave 局 its meaning 'bureau, office, situation.'
长 (simplified from 長) depicts an elderly figure with long flowing hair and a cane — length and seniority are linked in the original picture.

example.hanzi: 他被任命为新任局长。
example.pinyin: Tā bèi rènmìng wéi xīnrèn júzhǎng.
example.english: He was appointed as the new bureau chief.
example.fact: 长 (zhǎng, "head, chief") is a modular suffix that attaches to almost any organizational noun to name its leader — 局长 ("bureau chief"), 校长 ("school principal"), 部长 ("department minister") — all built the same way, so recognizing 长 as "the head of X" unlocks a whole family of job titles at once.

components.note: 纟 (silk thread) originally related to spinning thread to completion, extended to mean accomplishment.
责 (duty) sits beside the thread element, tying the idea of one's responsibilities to what gets accomplished, giving 绩 its meaning 'achievement.'

example.hanzi: 她这次考试的成绩很好。
example.pinyin: Tā zhè cì kǎoshì de chéngjì hěn hǎo.
example.english: Her grades on this exam are very good.
example.fact: 成绩 covers both a one-time test score and a longer-term track record of achievement — 这次考试的成绩 ("this exam's grade") and 工作成绩 ("job performance") use the exact same word, where English reaches for two different words, "grade" and "achievement/performance."

components.note: 弓 (bow) — a strong bow that took great force to draw gave 强 its meaning 'strong, powerful.'
虫 was a different phonetic element historically; its pronunciation has shifted so far from qiáng over time that the sound link is no longer obvious.
灬 (fire) — 烈 relates to something as intense and fierce as fire
列 (liè) gives the sound — an exact match with 烈's reading liè

example.hanzi: 大家对这个决定表示强烈反对。
example.pinyin: Dàjiā duì zhège juédìng biǎoshì qiángliè fǎnduì.
example.english: Everyone expressed strong opposition to this decision.
example.fact: 强烈 almost always modifies an abstract noun or verb of feeling or reaction — 强烈反对 ("strong opposition"), 强烈的感情 ("intense feelings") — while for a person's or object's physical strength, Chinese instead reaches for the plainer 强壮 or 强大.

components.note: 心 (heart/mind) — 意 relates to thought, intention, and meaning, things of the mind.
音 (yīn) is the historical phonetic element; its modern reading has drifted from yì, though both share a similar vowel.
口 (mouth) — 味 relates to taste, sensed in the mouth.
未 (wèi) gives the sound — an exact match with 味.

example.hanzi: 他的沉默似乎意味着什么。
example.pinyin: Tā de chénmò sìhū yìwèizhe shénme.
example.english: His silence seemed to imply something.
example.fact: 意味 as a verb almost never stands alone — it takes the aspect suffix 着 to form 意味着 ("to signify, to imply"), one of the most common ways Chinese frames "X means/implies Y" in writing and speech alike.

components.note: 壴 (a drum) — beating a drum in celebration
口 (mouth) — singing along in celebration
刂 (knife) contributes to the character's form, though its link to 剧's meaning 'drama' has faded over time.
居 (jū) gives a rhyme close to jù, with the tone shifted.

example.hanzi: 这部电影是一部很有趣的喜剧。
example.pinyin: Zhè bù diànyǐng shì yí bù hěn yǒuqù de xǐjù.
example.english: This movie is a very funny comedy.
example.fact: 喜剧 pairs 喜 ("joy," the same character that doubles up in 喜欢 in the pilot batch) with 剧 ("drama, play") for a transparent "joyful drama" — its direct opposite, 悲剧 ("tragedy"), swaps in 悲 ("sorrow") for the exact same structure.

components.note: A short stroke placed below a longer one — the mirror image of 上 (up), together forming a simple, opposite pair.

example.hanzi: 王子殿下今天将访问这座城市。
example.pinyin: Wángzǐ diànxià jīntiān jiāng fǎngwèn zhè zuò chéngshì.
example.english: His Royal Highness the prince will visit this city today.
example.fact: 殿下 literally means "below the palace hall" (殿, "palace hall" + 下, "below") — a self-effacing form of address that parallels 陛下 ("Your Majesty," literally "below the imperial steps") used for a reigning monarch, with 殿下 reserved for princes, princesses, and other highnesses one rank below.

meanings: to go to teach a class

components.note: A short stroke placed above a longer one — a simple graphic way to show 'up' or 'above,' contrasted with 下 (down), which flips the strokes.
讠 (speech) — 课 relates to lessons taught through spoken instruction.
果 (guǒ) gives a sound distantly related to kè, having drifted apart over time.

example.hanzi: 我们八点开始上课。
example.pinyin: Wǒmen bā diǎn kāishǐ shàngkè.
example.english: We start class at eight o'clock.
example.fact: 上 in 上课 carries the same "to engage with, to attend" sense as in 上班 ("to go to work") and 上网 ("to go online") — a single verb that turns whatever noun follows it into "to do the thing that noun is for," rather than its more literal meaning "to go up."

components.note: 艹 (grass) forms the top of the character.
木 (tree), sheltered beneath a covering, together depict plants flourishing, giving 荣 its meaning 'glory, prosperity.'
言 (word, speech) at the bottom shows this relates to spoken reputation.
兴 (to prosper, flourish) above shows praise for success, giving 誉 its meaning 'reputation, praise.'

example.hanzi: 获得这个奖项是一种荣誉。
example.pinyin: Huòdé zhège jiǎngxiàng shì yì zhǒng róngyù.
example.english: Winning this award is an honor.
example.fact: 荣 pictures grass 艹 and a tree 木 flourishing under cover, giving it the sense "to flourish, glory," while 誉 puts 言 ("speech") beside a growing 兴 ("to prosper") to mean "praise, reputation" — 荣誉 combines a picture of flourishing with a picture of praise into the abstract noun "honor."

components.note: 云 here stands in for an older form meaning "to speak of, to taste," 尝's core meaning.
尚 (shàng) gives a sound distantly related to cháng, having drifted apart over time.
云 here stands in for an older form meaning "to speak of, to taste," 尝's core meaning.
尚 (shàng) gives a sound distantly related to cháng, having drifted apart over time.

example.hanzi: 你尝尝这个汤,看看咸不咸。
example.pinyin: Nǐ chángchang zhège tāng, kànkan xián bu xián.
example.english: Try this soup and see if it's salty enough.
example.fact: 尝尝 reduplicates the single verb 尝 ("to taste") to make the action feel small, casual, and low-commitment — "just a quick taste" — the exact same softening pattern behind 看看 ("take a quick look") and 试试 ("give it a try"), both cited in the pilot batch as models for this pattern.

components.note: 讠 (speech) — relates to 设's meaning 'to establish, set up,' something first proposed through words.
殳 (shū) served as the phonetic base; its pronunciation has since drifted well away from shè.
讠 (speech) — 计 relates to counting or planning through words and numbers.
十 (shí) gives a hint of the sound — 计 is pronounced jì, a connection that has shifted significantly over time.
帀 (a banner or covering) — flying above the scene.
刂 (a knife) — wielded with skill beneath the banner, an image of expertise giving 师 its meaning 'master, teacher, expert.'

example.hanzi: 她是一位很有名的设计师。
example.pinyin: Tā shì yí wèi hěn yǒumíng de shèjìshī.
example.english: She is a very famous designer.
example.fact: 师 is a modular suffix meaning "master, practitioner of a craft" that turns almost any skilled activity into a job title — 设计 ("to design") + 师 gives 设计师 ("designer"), the same pattern behind 老师 ("teacher") and 厨师 ("chef").

components.note: 辶 (to walk) — 违 involves stepping away from what is required, i.e. disobeying.
韦 (wéi) is an exact match for the sound of 违.
厂 (a cliff or overhang) — 反 pictures pushing against a steep surface.
又 (a hand) — a hand pushing back against a cliff gave 反 its meaning 'to turn over' or 'opposite.'

example.hanzi: 这样做违反了公司的规定。
example.pinyin: Zhèyàng zuò wéifǎn le gōngsī de guīdìng.
example.english: Doing this violates the company's rules.
example.fact: 违反 almost always takes an abstract, rule-like object — a law, regulation, or principle (违反规定, "violate a rule") — while for physically breaking a concrete object, Chinese uses an entirely different verb, 打破 or 弄坏, a split English "violate" vs. "break" does not map onto directly.

components.note: 阝 (hill) — 阶 originally referred to steps built into a hillside or mound
介 (jiè) gives a sound close to 阶's reading jiē, sharing a similar historical pronunciation
段 shows 殳 (a hand wielding a tool) cutting or shaping stone into pieces — giving 段 its meaning 'section, segment, paragraph.'

example.hanzi: 这个项目已经进入了新的阶段。
example.pinyin: Zhège xiàngmù yǐjīng jìnrù le xīn de jiēduàn.
example.english: This project has already entered a new stage.
example.fact: 阶 (from 阝, "hill," plus a phonetic 介) originally referred to physical steps cut into a hillside, and 段 pictures a hand-held tool 殳 cutting something into a segment — 阶段 fuses "a step" with "a segment" into the abstract idea of one stage within a longer process.

components.note: 不 (not) — 否 relates directly to negation and denial
口 (kǒu) gives a loose sound connection to 否's reading fǒu
讠 (speech) — 认 relates to recognizing or acknowledging something, often expressed through words.
人 (rén) gives the sound — 认 is pronounced rèn, a close variant of the same sound.

example.hanzi: 他否认自己做过这件事。
example.pinyin: Tā fǒurèn zìjǐ zuòguo zhè jiàn shì.
example.english: He denied having done this.
example.fact: 否认 is built from 否 ("no, not so") plus 认 ("to acknowledge, recognize") — literally "to not-acknowledge" — and its near-opposite 承认 ("to admit, confess") swaps in 承 ("to bear, undertake") for the same 认 root, giving a matched pair of deny/admit verbs built the same way.

components.note: 冏 (bright, a window admitting light) — appears in 商's ancient form, though its exact link to 'commerce, to discuss' is unclear today.
章 — a graphic element whose original contribution to the character's meaning has been lost over time.
里 (a unit of distance, related to a village measure) — 量 relates to measuring quantity.
旦 (dàn) gives a hint of the sound — 量 is pronounced liàng, a connection that has shifted significantly over time.

example.hanzi: 我们得好好商量一下这件事。
example.pinyin: Wǒmen děi hǎohǎo shāngliang yíxià zhè jiàn shì.
example.english: We need to discuss this matter carefully.
example.fact: 商量 implies a mutual, back-and-forth negotiation between two or more people working toward a joint decision — closer to English "to talk something over" than the more one-directional 讨论 ("to discuss, debate"), which can just as easily describe one person analyzing a topic alone.

components.note: 亻 (person) — 什 originally referred to a group of people.
十 (ten) — combined with 亻 (person), 什 originally described a group of ten; the character later came to be used for the common word 什么 (what).

example.hanzi: 桌子上有书、笔什么的。
example.pinyin: Zhuōzi shàng yǒu shū, bǐ shénme de.
example.english: There are books, pens, and so on, on the table.
example.fact: 什么的 always closes out a list rather than opening one, tacked onto the final item to mean "...and so on" — functioning much like English "etc.," but built from two pieces reused elsewhere with unrelated senses: the question word 什么 ("what") and the particle 的.

components.note: 屮 (a young sprout) growing up and out of 凵 (a container or pit) — a picture of something emerging, hence 'going out.'

example.hanzi: 他这么做完全是出于好意。
example.pinyin: Tā zhème zuò wánquán shì chūyú hǎoyì.
example.english: He did this entirely out of good intentions.
example.fact: 出于 always names a motive or origin right after it — 出于好意 ("out of good intentions"), 出于礼貌 ("out of politeness") — pairing the verb 出 ("to come out of") with the preposition 于 ("from, at") into a fixed phrase that works much like English "out of" before a reason.

components.note: 立 (to stand) — 站 relates to standing, and by extension a stop or station where one stands to wait
占 (zhàn) gives the sound — 站 is also pronounced zhàn, an exact match
亻 (person) — the one settling somewhere.
主 (host, master) — the idea of a person settled in a place as if hosting it, giving 住 its meaning 'to live, reside, stay.'

example.hanzi: 警察大喊:“站住!”
example.pinyin: Jǐngchá dà hǎn: “Zhànzhù!”
example.english: The police shouted, "Stop!"
example.fact: 住 attached after a verb often marks that an action holds firmly in place — 站住 ("stop and stay put," literally "stand-hold"), 记住 ("to remember," literally "remember-hold") — a common verb-complement pattern where 住 contributes "staying fixed" rather than its literal sense "to live, reside."

components.note: The character traces the front view of an ox's head, with the top stroke and crossing lines representing its curved horns and ears.
亻 (person) on the left represents someone tending to something small.
子 (child) on the right depicts the small, young thing being watched over, giving 仔 its meaning of something small or young.

example.hanzi: 电影里的牛仔骑着马进了城。
example.pinyin: Diànyǐng lǐ de niúzǎi qízhe mǎ jìn le chéng.
example.english: The cowboy in the movie rode into town on his horse.
example.fact: 牛仔 literally means "cattle kid" (牛, "cattle" + 仔, "young one, kid") — a fittingly literal name for someone who herds cattle for a living — and the same word, shortened, gives 牛仔裤 ("cowboy pants," i.e. jeans) and 牛仔布 ("denim").

components.note: 十 (here representing a weapon or armor) — 克 pictures overcoming an opponent.
兄 (a person, here representing a formidable figure) — overcoming a strong opponent gave 克 its meaning 'to overcome' or 'to be able to.'

example.hanzi: 我的朋友尼克来自美国。
example.pinyin: Wǒ de péngyou Níkè láizì Měiguó.
example.english: My friend Nick is from America.
example.fact: 尼克 is a pure phonetic transliteration of the English name "Nick" — neither 尼 nor 克 contributes any of its own meaning here, the same way 克 is reused purely for its sound in other transliterated names in this batch, like 克莱尔 ("Claire").

components.note: 禾 (a grain plant) — a sweet-smelling crop
日 — here standing in for sweetness (originally 甘), giving the sense of a pleasant smell
木 (tree) — 槟 names the areca palm and its nut.
宾 (bīn) gives an exact match for 槟's reading.

example.hanzi: 他们打开了一瓶香槟庆祝。
example.pinyin: Tāmen dǎkāi le yì píng xiāngbīn qìngzhù.
example.english: They opened a bottle of champagne to celebrate.
example.fact: 香槟 is a phono-semantic loanword: 槟 was chosen mainly to approximate the sound "-pagne" (bīn), while 香 ("fragrant") fits the drink's aroma — a common strategy in Chinese for borrowing foreign words, blending sound-matching with a sense-appropriate character.

meanings: to steal and make off with

components.note: 亻 (person) — 偷 describes a person's action, stealing.
俞 (yú) gives a sound distantly related to tōu, having drifted apart over time.
土 (here representing a person swinging their arms, not its usual meaning 'earth') — depicts someone in motion.
止 (a foot) — combined with the moving figure above, 走 shows a person walking or running.

example.hanzi: 有人把我的自行车偷走了。
example.pinyin: Yǒurén bǎ wǒ de zìxíngchē tōuzǒu le.
example.english: Someone stole my bicycle.
example.fact: 走 attached after a verb often marks "away, off" as the direction the action carries something — 偷走 ("to steal away"), 拿走 ("to take away") — a directional-complement pattern that turns a plain verb into "verb + and remove it," distinct from 走 standing alone to mean simply "to walk."

components.note: 艹 (grass/plant) — 艺 originally related to planting and cultivating skillfully
乙 (yǐ) gives a sound distantly related to 艺's reading yì, having drifted apart over time
宀 (roof) — 家 is about a home, the space under a roof.
豕 (shǐ, 'pig') supplies the ancient sound for 家; keeping a pig under one's roof was also a practical sign of a household in ancient China, though the modern readings jiā and shǐ no longer rhyme.

example.hanzi: 他从小就想成为一名艺术家。
example.pinyin: Tā cóngxiǎo jiù xiǎng chéngwéi yì míng yìshùjiā.
example.english: Ever since he was little, he's wanted to become an artist.
example.fact: 家 as a suffix meaning "an expert or practitioner of X" turns 艺术 ("art") into 艺术家 ("artist"), the same pattern behind 科学家 ("scientist") and 音乐家 ("musician") — a more prestigious-sounding suffix than the plainer 师 seen elsewhere in this batch, as in 设计师 ("designer").

components.note: 尸, here a variant of 厂, depicts a roof or shelter.
至 depicts arriving or coming to rest — settling under a roof gave 屋 its meaning 'house, room.'
田 (farmland) over 土 (earth/soil) — originally referred to a village or a measured unit of farmland, later extended to mean 'inside' or a unit of distance.

example.hanzi: 外面很冷,快到屋里来吧。
example.pinyin: Wàimiàn hěn lěng, kuài dào wūlǐ lái ba.
example.english: It's cold outside, come inside quickly.
example.fact: 屋里 attaches the locational suffix 里 ("inside") directly to 屋 ("room, house") to mean "indoors" — the same 里 that turns 这 into 这里 ("here") elsewhere in this deck, here doing the same job of turning a plain noun into a place word.

components.note: 十 (here representing a weapon or armor) — 克 pictures overcoming an opponent.
兄 (a person, here representing a formidable figure) — overcoming a strong opponent gave 克 its meaning 'to overcome' or 'to be able to.'
艹 (grass) — 莱 names a weedy plant, goosefoot.
来 (lái) is an exact match for the sound of 莱.

example.hanzi: 克莱尔是我们班最聪明的学生。
example.pinyin: Kèláiěr shì wǒmen bān zuì cōngmíng de xuésheng.
example.english: Claire is the smartest student in our class.
example.fact: Each syllable of 克莱尔 was chosen purely to approximate the English name "Claire" phonetically — none of the three characters' own literal meanings ("to overcome," a weedy plant, an old pronoun) has anything to do with the name itself, a hallmark of Chinese transliterated foreign names.

components.note: 扌 (hand) — relates to 技's meaning 'skill, technique,' a skill performed with the hands.
支 (zhī) served as the phonetic base; its pronunciation has since drifted well away from jì.
工 (work, tool) — 巧 relates to skill in craft or work.
丂 (kǎo) gives a sound close to qiǎo.

example.hanzi: 弹好这首曲子需要一些技巧。
example.pinyin: Tán hǎo zhè shǒu qǔzi xūyào yìxiē jìqiǎo.
example.english: Playing this piece well requires some technique.
example.fact: 技巧 leans toward a practiced, hands-on skill or trick of the craft — a musician's fingering, a photographer's framing — while its broader cousin 技术 ("technology, technique") covers systematic, often more formally trained expertise, a distinction that does not survive translation into the single English word "skill."

components.note: 忄 (heart) — 情 relates to feelings and emotions.
青 (qīng) gives the sound — 情 is pronounced qíng, a close match differing only in tone.
咸 (all, together) — 感 relates to a shared reaction.
心 (heart) — feelings that stir the heart gave 感 its meaning 'to feel' or 'emotion.'

example.hanzi: 这首诗表达了作者深厚的情感。
example.pinyin: Zhè shǒu shī biǎodá le zuòzhě shēnhòu de qínggǎn.
example.english: This poem expresses the poet's deep emotion.
example.fact: 情感 leans toward a more literary or analytical register than the everyday, spoken 感情 — the two characters simply swap order — much as English sometimes prefers "affect" over "feelings" in a clinical or academic context.

components.note: A vertical line 丨 running through the middle of a box or flag 口 — a simple image for the idea of 'center, middle.'

example.hanzi: 那张桌子放在房间的中央。
example.pinyin: Nà zhāng zhuōzi fàng zài fángjiān de zhōngyāng.
example.english: That table is placed in the center of the room.
example.fact: 中央 can name either a literal physical center (房间的中央, "the center of the room") or the central government or leadership of an organization (中央政府) — a split that English marks by capitalizing "Central" only in the second, institutional sense.

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 提 relates to lifting or carrying something by hand.
是 (shì) gives a hint of the sound — 提 is pronounced tí, a connection that has shifted over time.
讠 (speech) — relates to 议's meaning 'to discuss, deliberate; opinion.'
义 (yì) gives the sound — 议 is also pronounced yì, an exact match.

example.hanzi: 有人提议下周去爬山。
example.pinyin: Yǒurén tíyì xià zhōu qù páshān.
example.english: Someone proposed going hiking next week.
example.fact: 提议 pairs 提 ("to lift, raise") with 议 ("to discuss, deliberate") for a literal "to raise for discussion" — it works as both a verb ("to propose") and a noun ("a proposal") with no change in form, the same free verb/noun flexibility seen in 工作 in the pilot batch.

components.note: 辶 (to walk) — 逃 means to escape or flee, involving movement.
兆 (zhào) gives a rhyme close to táo, with the initial shifted.
辶 (to walk) — 避 means to avoid, moving away from something.
辟 (bì) gives the sound — an exact match with 避.

example.hanzi: 他总是逃避责任。
example.pinyin: Tā zǒngshì táobì zérèn.
example.english: He always avoids responsibility.
example.fact: 逃避 doubles up two verbs that both mean roughly "to flee, avoid" — 逃 ("to escape, flee") and 避 ("to avoid, dodge") — with a slightly disapproving tone, unlike the neutral 避免 ("to avoid"), making 逃避 the word of choice specifically for shirking a duty or facing something one should confront.

components.note: 母 (mǔ, 'mother') serves as the phonetic base; the sound has since diverged from měi, so the connection is mostly historical today.
冂 depicts a boundary or border enclosing an area.
土 (earth/land) — the land enclosed within the border.
口 here depicts a well within that land — together giving 周 its early meaning of a bounded territory, and later 'circumference, week, the Zhou dynasty.'

example.hanzi: 我们每周去一次超市。
example.pinyin: Wǒmen měi zhōu qù yí cì chāoshì.
example.english: We go to the supermarket once a week.
example.fact: 每 ("each, every") attaches to a whole family of time-unit words the same way — 每天 ("every day"), 每月 ("every month"), 每周 ("every week") — a single, reusable prefix standing in for English's separate constructions "every day/week/month."

components.note: 罒 (a net) — the law closing in around wrongdoing
非 (wrong) — the wrongdoing itself, caught in the net
夕 (evening, night) — in the dark, one could not see a person's face, so calling out their name was necessary to identify them.
口 (mouth) — calling out with the mouth at night gave 名 its meaning 'name.'

example.hanzi: 他因盗窃罪名被捕。
example.pinyin: Tā yīn dàoqiè zuìmíng bèi bǔ.
example.english: He was arrested on a charge of theft.
example.fact: 罪 pictures a net 罒 closing over wrongdoing 非, and 名 pictures calling out with the mouth 口 in the dark 夕 to identify someone — 罪名 fuses "the crime" with "the name for it" into the formal legal term for a specific charge, distinct from 罪 alone, which can mean the broader concept of guilt or sin.

components.note: 行 (to go/walk) — 街 names a road where people walk and travel.
圭 (guī) gives a sound distantly related to jiē, having drifted apart over time.
匸 (an enclosure or boundary) — 区 pictures a defined territory.
乂 (a mark, here representing control or division) — dividing land into bounded territories gave 区 its meaning 'district' or 'area.'

example.hanzi: 这个街区最近新开了不少餐厅。
example.pinyin: Zhège jiēqū zuìjìn xīn kāi le bù shǎo cāntīng.
example.english: A lot of new restaurants have opened in this neighborhood recently.
example.fact: 街区 combines 街 ("street") with 区 ("district, zone") into a unit of urban geography roughly matching the English "city block" or "neighborhood" — a distinctly modern, planning-oriented word, unlike the older, more conversational 街上 ("on the street") for describing the same physical space.

components.note: 辶 (to walk) — 道 relates to a path or road one walks along.
首 (shǒu) is the historical phonetic element; its modern reading no longer resembles dào, a reminder that sound components can drift after thousands of years of pronunciation change.

example.hanzi: 你最喜欢看哪个频道?
example.pinyin: Nǐ zuì xǐhuan kàn nǎge píndào?
example.english: Which channel do you like watching the most?
example.fact: 频道 was coined for broadcast technology by combining 频 ("frequency," from radio-wave frequency) with 道 ("path, way," the same 道 that underlies 知道 in the pilot batch) — literally "a frequency path," giving Chinese its own compositional word for "channel" rather than a phonetic loan.

components.note: 日 (sun/day) — relates to 时's meaning of 'time, season'; the phonetic part of the character was later replaced by 寸 in the simplified form
月 (moon) — 期 relates to time measured by the moon's cycles, like a period or term.
其 (qí) gives a hint of the sound — 期 is pronounced qī, a connection that has shifted slightly in tone.

example.hanzi: 这是历史上一个重要的时期。
example.pinyin: Zhè shì lìshǐ shàng yí gè zhòngyào de shíqī.
example.english: This is an important period in history.
example.fact: 时期 names a stretch of history or a broader era (历史时期, "historical period") in a more formal, written register than the everyday 时候 seen in the pilot batch, which almost always marks one specific personal moment inside a "...的时候" clause rather than a sweeping span of time.

components.note: 八 here depicts something splitting apart or being divided.
厶 is an old form meaning 'private' or 'one's own' — 公 shows dividing up private property to share it fairly, giving rise to the meaning 'public' or 'fair.'
八 (a hand shape) — one of two hands shown reaching toward the same object.
廾 (two hands together) — jointly holding up one object, giving 共 its meaning 'together, joint, common.'

example.hanzi: 请不要在公共场所大声说话。
example.pinyin: Qǐng bú yào zài gōnggòng chǎngsuǒ dàshēng shuōhuà.
example.english: Please don't talk loudly in public places.
example.fact: 公 alone already carries the sense "fair, shared, not private" (as in 公平, "fair"), and 共 alone means "together, joint" — 公共 doubles up two overlapping "shared" characters into the modern adjective "public," the same reinforcing word-building strategy behind 喜欢 in the pilot batch.

components.note: 牛 (ox/cattle) — cattle were among the earliest and most valuable kinds of property, connecting 物 to the general idea of 'object' or 'thing.'
勿 (wù) gives the sound — 物 is also pronounced wù, an exact match.
贝 (shell, an ancient form of currency) — 质 originally meant 'pledge, hostage,' something valuable given as a guarantee, extended to 'quality, substance, nature.'
十 (shí) served as the phonetic base; its pronunciation has since drifted well away from zhì.

example.hanzi: 水是生命必需的物质。
example.pinyin: Shuǐ shì shēngmìng bìxū de wùzhì.
example.english: Water is a substance essential to life.
example.fact: 物质 covers both the scientific sense "matter, substance" and the everyday sense "material things, material comfort" (as in 物质生活, "material life") — a single word spanning a chemistry classroom and a conversation about worldly possessions, where English keeps "matter" and "material" further apart.

meanings: to repeat from mouth to mouth

components.note: 亻 (person) — relates to 传's meaning 'to pass on, transmit,' something passed from person to person.
专 (zhuān) gives a sound hint — 传 is pronounced chuán, sharing the same rhyme though the initial consonant differs.
讠 (speech radical) — shows 说 relates to talking or language
兑 (duì) is the phonetic component; historically 说 was also pronounced closer to 兑's sound before shifting to shuō

example.hanzi: 这是一个古老的传说。
example.pinyin: Zhè shì yí gè gǔlǎo de chuánshuō.
example.english: This is an ancient legend.
example.fact: 传说 literally means "to pass on by speaking" (传, "to transmit" + 说, "to speak") — as a noun it names the legend itself, and placed at the start of a sentence (传说..., "legend has it that...") it introduces a claim whose source is folklore rather than verified fact.

components.note: 身 — depicts a drawn bow
寸 — a hand releasing the arrow
手 (hand) — in the traditional form 擊, 手 contributed the meaning of striking with force, the source of 击's meaning 'to hit, strike.'

example.hanzi: 他在射击比赛中获得了第一名。
example.pinyin: Tā zài shèjī bǐsài zhōng huòdé le dì yī míng.
example.english: He won first place in the shooting competition.
example.fact: 射 already pictures the whole action on its own — 身 (a drawn bow) and 寸 (a hand releasing it) — so 击 ("to strike, hit") mostly reinforces the sense of forceful impact; 射击 as a compound is reserved for firearms and target shooting, distinct from 射 alone, which also covers shooting an arrow or, more abstractly, casting a glance.

components.note: 卩 (a kneeling figure) — a hungry person kneeling down, about to eat.
皀 (a bowl of food) — the meal in front of them, giving 即 its sense of imminent action, 'right away, that is to say.'

example.hanzi: 即便下雨,我们也要出发。
example.pinyin: Jíbiàn xiàyǔ, wǒmen yě yào chūfā.
example.english: Even if it rains, we still have to set out.
example.fact: 即便 is always the setup half of a two-part sentence completed by 也 ("still, also") — 即便...,也... — functioning as a more formal, written-register synonym for the everyday 就算...,也... and 即使...,也..., all three built on the same "even if...still..." template.

components.note: 目 (eye) — 眼 refers directly to the eye itself.
艮 (gèn) gives a sound hint — 眼 is pronounced yǎn; the rhyme has drifted apart over the centuries.
钅 (metal) — early mirrors were made of polished bronze.
竟 (jìng) is an exact match for the sound of 镜.

example.hanzi: 他戴着一副眼镜。
example.pinyin: Tā dàizhe yí fù yǎnjìng.
example.english: He is wearing a pair of glasses.
example.fact: 眼镜 pairs 眼 ("eye") with 镜 ("mirror," built on the metal radical 钅, since early mirrors were polished bronze) — literally "eye mirror," the same logic behind English "looking glass" — and its measure word is 副 ("a pair, a set"), the same classifier used for gloves and a deck of playing cards.

components.note: 心 (heart) — 愿 relates to a heartfelt wish or desire
原 (yuán) gives a loose sound connection to 愿's reading yuàn
Depicts a person standing tall, gazing up at the moon 月 — the image of looking into the distance, the source of 望's meaning 'to gaze, hope, expect.'

example.hanzi: 她的愿望是环游世界。
example.pinyin: Tā de yuànwàng shì huányóu shìjiè.
example.english: Her wish is to travel around the world.
example.fact: 愿 (built from 心, "heart," plus a phonetic 原) contributes "a heartfelt wish," and 望 pictures someone gazing up at the moon 月 in the distance, "to hope, to gaze toward" — 愿望 fuses wishing with gazing toward into a noun for a hope one holds and looks forward to, stronger and more aspirational than the plain verb 想要 ("to want").

components.note: 尸, here a variant of 厂, depicts a roof or shelter.
至 depicts arriving or coming to rest — settling under a roof gave 屋 its meaning 'house, room.'
页 (head) — 顶 names the top of the head, the crown.
丁 (dīng) gives the sound — an exact match with 顶.

example.hanzi: 雨落在屋顶上,发出轻轻的声音。
example.pinyin: Yǔ luò zài wūdǐng shàng, fāchū qīngqīng de shēngyīn.
example.english: Rain fell on the roof, making a soft sound.
example.fact: 顶 already means "the very top" on its own — the top of a head, a mountain, a container — so 屋顶 ("roof") is transparently "the top of the house," the same 顶 that also gives 山顶 ("mountaintop") and 头顶 ("the top of one's head").

components.note: 走 (to walk/run) — 起 relates to standing up and setting into motion.
己 (jǐ) gives a close sound cue — 起 is pronounced qǐ, sharing the same final sound.
广 (shelter) suggests a piece of furniture kept indoors.
木 (wood) — early beds were built from wood, giving 床 its meaning.

example.hanzi: 我每天早上七点起床。
example.pinyin: Wǒ měitiān zǎoshang qī diǎn qǐchuáng.
example.english: I get up at seven every morning.
example.fact: 起床 literally combines 起 ("to rise," the same 起 seen in 起来 and 一起 in the pilot batch) with 床 ("bed") for "to rise from bed" — its natural opposite is 上床 ("to go to bed," literally "to get onto the bed"), a matched pair built the same simple way.

components.note: 兔 depicts a rabbit's body with long ears and a short tail, seen in profile.
A simple drawing of a swaddled baby — arms reaching out, legs bundled together in a wrap.

example.hanzi: 花园里有一只白色的兔子。
example.pinyin: Huāyuán lǐ yǒu yì zhī báisè de tùzi.
example.english: There is a white rabbit in the garden.
example.fact: 子 in 兔子 is a light, semantically empty noun suffix rather than a meaningful "child" — the same suffix pattern seen in 孩子 in the pilot batch, though there 子 also happens to independently mean "child," while here in 兔子 it is purely grammatical filler with no connection to baby rabbits.
